claims.text: In monometallic transition-metal catalysts, surface strain governs catalytic activity and selectivity by tuning the d-band center.
Tensile surface strain shifts the d-band center upward.
Compressive surface strain shifts the d-band center downward.
An upward shift of the d-band center strengthens adsorption of key reaction intermediates.
A downward shift of the d-band center weakens adsorption of key reaction intermediates.
Strain-induced changes in intermediate adsorption affect turnover frequency and product selectivity.
Substrate-induced epitaxial growth or mechanical bending can introduce controlled tensile or compressive surface strain.
Surface strain changes interatomic distances in the catalyst surface.
Strain-induced changes in interatomic distance alter the local d-band electronic structure of active metal atoms.
Tensile strain can increase catalytic turnover when stronger intermediate adsorption is beneficial to the selected reaction.
Compressive strain should produce weaker adsorption and either lower activity or altered selectivity relative to an unstrained catalyst.
The proposed strain effect should hold when electronic factors dominate and significant surface reconstruction or oxidation is absent.
The magnitude of the d-band shift, adsorption-energy change, and catalytic-performance change depends on the metal and strain magnitude.
Surface-sensitive spectroscopy such as XPS or infrared spectroscopy can assess the proposed strain-induced change in the d-band center.
